style: calm, natural hesitations, like explaining to a friend
slides: Now, a danger.
Some weakenings look like weakenings, but they actually hurt you. I call them weak weakenings.
Usually, it's better not to use them.
A weak weakening sounds like an answer, but it actually shows the reader poor critical thinking.
We'll see three of them. The short blanket, extremism, and the slippery slope.
In chain terms, a weak weakening either attacks an arrow that's actually strong... or it invents arrows the other side never drew.
First, the principle of the short blanket. Don't try to solve problems by ignoring it.
If I have a short blanket, and I pull it up to cover my head... my feet are left uncovered.
Say I'm arguing for privacy, against the cameras. I write: true, citizens' lives have to be protected, but let the state do it in a different way. Put more police officers on the street.
Now, it is a weakening. I gave the other side a solution.
But it shows very low critical thinking. It's a short blanket. Police officers cost money. So where does that money come from?
I take it from somewhere else. So I solved one problem, and created a problem in another place.
It's not clever to say: fine, let's just bring the money from nowhere.
There's a disease. Okay, let's add its drug to the list of medicines the state pays for.
Wait. So what do I take off that list? You can't just create something from nothing.
Ignoring the short-blanket principle shows very, very low critical thinking. A lot of students do it. Don't.
The next one. Extremism.
Reduced tax for large companies. Someone says: wait, who decided what a large company is?
They'll start giving reduced tax to all the companies, every single one, and in the end the state will have no money at all.
This is when someone becomes a bit of a drama queen. Extreme. What if it happens all the way, to everyone? Come on. There's no need to be extreme.
It's not a realistic argument. You don't really believe the state will give reduced tax to every company and collect no tax at all.
And there's something else hiding behind an extreme weakening.
What is that person actually saying? 'Right now, I have no problem with your position. I'm just afraid that if it gets extreme, there'll be a problem.'
Well, how nice. With that extreme weakening, he's really saying: your position is fine. Reduced tax for large companies is fine. I'm just afraid it'll spread to lots of smaller companies too.
So all I need to say is: don't worry. I understand your concern. Let's put in a safeguard. Let's set a threshold, say, a thousand employees or more. No problem.
That's why an extreme weakening isn't a good one. And by the way, extremism is a bad thing in almost every area of life.
Another weakening that causes trouble: the slippery slope. It's also a kind of extremism.
With extremism, we stayed in the same field, and only exaggerated the effect. A tax cut for some companies becomes a tax cut for all of them.
On a slippery slope, you slide further and further, into other things.

Today you put cameras in public space? Tomorrow you'll put them in private space. And the day after, you'll listen inside our homes and follow our e-mails and messages, because maybe someone is planning an offence there.
Again, a bit of a drama queen. It's not really realistic that this is what will happen.

In chain terms, a slippery slope is a chain where nobody tested the arrows. Why would cameras in public space lead to listening inside homes? Each step would need its own decision, and its own reason.
And just like with extremism, between the lines he's admitting that cameras in public space are fine. So let's make sure it doesn't slide further. Put a brake in place.
We're discussing this proposal now. Not what might happen someday.
Now, the psychological side of finding weakenings.
Very often, we look at a counter-argument and say: it's right. It has no holes. I can't weaken it. All I can do is say that mine matters more.
So first of all, remember. There's almost never a situation with no way out.
I've been in so many situations that seemed closed from every direction. And then we sat, we thought, we turned it over, looked at it from different angles... and suddenly we found a way around.
So even if an argument seems airtight, push yourself. Wait, keep looking. It's usually not that there's no way out. You just need to be really creative to find it.
And when you're stuck, write their chain, and question every arrow, one by one. That's often where the way out shows up.
Another thing. Don't be rigid. A rigid mind takes a more extreme position than it really holds, and it can't see the weak links in its own position.
So look for weakenings of your own arguments too. Because the other side will definitely raise them.

A technique for that: devil's advocate. With a friend, or on your own. If I were on the other side, how would I weaken this? Really put some thought into it. The next lesson turns this into exercises.
